title: Acute Ischemic & Hemorrhagic Stroke: The Neuro-Ophthalmologist's Guide
summary: Stroke remains a leading cause of long-term disability, necessitating rapid identification of neuro-ophthalmic manifestations like visual field deficits and cranial nerve palsies. This guide integrates emergency triage with the high-yield clinical pearls essential for every ophthalmologist.

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Sudden onset monocular or binocular vision loss
Diplopia with cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, VI)

content.explanation: Face (droop), Arm (drift), Speech (slurred), Time (to ER). EYE: Check for sudden visual field cuts or diplopia.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Pathway
content: Step 1: Non-contrast CT Head (Rule out hemorrhage)
Step 2: CTA or MRA (Evaluate vessel patency)
Step 3: MRI DWI/ADC (Gold standard for acute ischemia)
Step 5: Carotid Doppler / Blood pressure management

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls for Ophthalmologists
content: Homonymous hemianopia: Respects the vertical meridian; implies retro-chiasmal lesion (look for stroke).
Ipsilateral Horner + Pain = Dissection until proven otherwise (Get CT Angio Neck).
Ocular Ischemic Syndrome: Presents with venous stasis retinopathy and mid-peripheral dot-blot hemorrhages; indicates severe carotid stenosis.
CRAO: Always check for underlying giant cell arteritis (ESR/CRP) or embolic source.
Treatment window for tPA (Alteplase) is generally < 4.5 hours from symptom onset.

sections.title: Management Principles
sections.content: For ischemic stroke: Intravenous thrombolysis (Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg) if within window. Mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusions (LVO) of the anterior circulation. Secondary prevention involves antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin, Clopidogrel) or anticoagulation for cardioembolic sources. Strict blood pressure control and lipid-lowering therapy (statins) are non-negotiable for long-term prognosis.
